prompt: According to Ehnert et al. (2016), sustainable HRM differs from strategic HRM mainly because it:

options.text: Pursues financial, social and ecological goals over a long-term horizon, inside and outside the firm
Replaces financial goals with social goals
Is the responsibility of the HR department only

explanation: Triple goals, inside and outside, long term, controlling side effects.

prompt: A company introduces a living-wage commitment for all suppliers although no law requires it, because it fits its values. This is an example of which motive (Stahl et al., 2020)?
explanation: Beyond the law and driven by the firm's values = mission-led.

prompt: An HR department ignores repeated harassment complaints in one plant. In Brewster & Brookes' (2024) terms this is:
explanation: HR fails to prevent a problem = omission.

prompt: In the Harvard Model (Beer et al., 1984), commitment, competence, congruence and cost-effectiveness are:
explanation: The 4 Cs are HR outcomes; long-term consequences are individual, organisational and societal well-being.

prompt: The best-fit (contingency) approach argues that:

options.text: One bundle of HR practices works in every firm
HR practices must match the organisation's strategy and context
Control is always better than commitment

explanation: Matching model (Jackson & Schuler, 1984).

prompt: Two candidates have equal grades, but one completed unpaid internships abroad arranged by family contacts. In Bourdieu's terms, these experiences mainly reflect:
explanation: Unpaid internships = money (economic capital); family contacts = networks (social capital).

prompt: According to signalling theory (Baron & Kreps, 1999), degrees are useful signals because they are:

options.text: Expensive to obtain, granted by screening institutions and require learning

explanation: But signals can be biased – weight them by how they were produced.

prompt: Why do field experiments (Quillian et al., 2019) allow conclusions about discrimination that data on real applicants cannot?

options.text: Applications are equivalent except for the group cue, so callback gaps are caused by the cue

explanation: Causal inference: only the cue differs.

prompt: A structured interview with a scoring rubric used by all interviewers mainly improves:
explanation: Same questions and scoring → consistent results across raters (reliability); it also supports validity.

prompt: Assessment centres for 3,000 applicants to seasonal shop jobs are problematic mainly because of low:
explanation: Too costly and slow for the volume and the job – practicability.

prompt: Kerr's “On the folly of rewarding A, while hoping for B” warns that organisations often:

options.text: Reward behaviours that differ from the ones they actually want

explanation: E.g. rewarding billable hours while hoping for collaboration.

prompt: Which element must a performance theory specify according to Latham, Sulsky & Macdonald (2007)?

options.text: Whether performance is compared with absolute standards or with peers

explanation: Dimensions, standards, situational constraints, number of levels, absolute vs relative.

prompt: Paying a software engineer more because few engineers are available on the labour market reflects:
explanation: Supply and demand / market pricing = external competitiveness (Renard, 2008).

prompt: At Safelite, piece rates increased productivity. Which condition helped most?

options.text: Output was easy to measure per worker and defects had to be fixed without pay
Workers were rewarded for team results only
Bonuses were paid ten years later
Managers decided bonuses at their discretion

explanation: Cheap measurement, individual control, quality protected by unpaid rework (Lazear, 2000).

prompt: According to Sayre et al. (2026), the main source of harm in pay-for-performance schemes is:

options.text: The existence of a base salary
Uncertainty about what is rewarded and how much employees will earn

explanation: Uncertainty → insecurity → overwork → stress and burnout.

prompt: A collective bonus based on the whole company's profit mainly risks weakening:

options.text: Line of sight between individual effort and reward

explanation: Trade-off alignment vs line of sight (expectancy); also free riding.

prompt: In Herzberg's two-factor model, compensation is a:

options.text: Hygiene factor whose absence creates dissatisfaction

explanation: Pay prevents dissatisfaction; motivators are achievement, recognition, work itself, responsibility, growth.

prompt: Under the EU pay transparency directive, an employer may NOT:

options.text: Give applicants a pay range before employment
Ask candidates about their salary history

explanation: Salary-history questions are banned; the others are required or allowed.

prompt: In Mortensen & Edmondson's (2023) holistic EVP, offering mentoring and clear career paths belongs to:
explanation: Learning and careers = growth & development.

prompt: A retailer's employer-brand campaign shows happy, diverse teams, but employees describe high pressure and little support. Which brand quality is violated most?
explanation: Consistent = the brand delivers against its promises (identity ≠ image).

prompt: Velora's bonus for warehouse team leaders is not producing the expected results. Based on the theories and concepts studied in class, explain why the scheme fails to motivate and is perceived as unfair.
modelAnswer: Expectancy theory: expectancy is weak because parcels per hour depend on season, client mix and the temporary staff head office assigns – not mainly on the team leader's effort; instrumentality is weak because the ranking can be adjusted “for attitude” and criteria are unwritten; valence is high (20 %) but only for three people. Sayre et al. (2026): relative, monthly, discretionary pay creates high uncertainty about what is rewarded and how much → insecurity, stress, “a lottery”, exits. Kerr / direction: rewarding speed while hoping for quality and cooperation → error rates rise and team leaders stop lending staff (forced-distribution effects: infighting, no collaboration, short-termism). Groysberg: direction wrong, fairness low (discretion, winner-takes-all), workability simple but costly through errors and turnover. Equity theory and pay transparency: team leaders compare outcomes/inputs with peers who win through luck or the manager's favour; the unexplained 11 % gender gap breaks internal consistency and cannot be justified under the EU pay transparency directive (≥ 5 % unexplained gap → joint pay assessment).
keyPoints: Expectancy and instrumentality broken with case facts
Kerr/direction: speed vs quality, no cooperation

prompt: Drawing on at least two theoretical frameworks, discuss the drawbacks of recruitment and selection at Velora's Amsterdam hub and propose an alternative approach that is both valid and inclusive.
modelAnswer: Drawbacks: (1) Signals and capitals – screening by university prestige relies on signals produced by economic, social and cultural capital (Bourdieu, Baron & Kreps) and misses job-relevant capability. (2) Bias – referrals and “fit with the team” = in-group favouritism and similar-to-me bias; the AI tool trained on current top performers reproduces past homogeneity (algorithmically biased recruitment = sin of commission); the outcome (young men from three universities) is inequality and possibly discrimination – testable with a field-experiment logic. (3) Validity, reliability, practicability – informal interviews have low reliability and validity; the AI shortlist is practicable but of unproven validity. (4) Psychological contract / realistic preview – one in three hires leaves because the job was “not what was described”. Alternative: job analysis → explicit criteria set in advance; recruitment through wider channels (several universities, bootcamps, communities, targeted outreach to under-represented groups), gender-neutral ads, a realistic job preview and an EVP the hub can deliver; selection with a work sample/technical test, structured competency interviews scored by diverse trained panels, fit defined as job-relevant values; audit the AI tool for validity and bias and keep human judgement; monitor diversity and retention data. Trade-off: more cost and time per hire, but better validity, diversity (innovation, Mohammadi et al.) and lower turnover.
